newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Volcano pelts Montserrat with rock, fire in capital.
newsitem.headline: Volcano pelts Montserrat with rock, fire in capital.

text.p: Hundreds of residents were evacuated on Tuesday from Montserrat's central region as the Soufriere Hills volcano pelted the island with ash and debris and fires raged in the abandoned capital.

Explosive eruptions on Monday night and early on Tuesday sent cascades of ash and volcanic pebbles over the British colony, and flows of red-hot rock, ash and gases rushed into Plymouth, setting fire to landmark buildings, officials said.
"It looks like a snow avalanche in Plymouth," government information officer Richard Aspin said.

The fires cast a red glow in the night sky over Plymouth. Officials said the new government headquarters, the technical college, police headquarters, the customs office and the public market were on fire and would be allowed to burn to the ground because the town was too dangerous for firefighters.
The government ordered some 700 residents to leave the island's central zone because of the rain of volcanic debris, which forced the closure of the seaside Vue Pointe hotel.
Many residents spent the night in their cars in the northern "safe zone" after fleeing the storm of ash and marble-sized pebbles, Aspin said.

The rumbling volcano for the second consecutive day sent pyroclastic flows of hot rock, ash and gases into Plymouth, the capital, abandoned during a major evacuation of the island's south end in April 1996.
The explosive eruptions from the volcano sent clouds of ashy gas and a shower of pumice-like pebbles into the atmosphere, darkening the sky.
Volcanic ash dusted revellers at carnivals on the nearby islands of Nevis, 30 miles (48 km) to the northwest and Antigua, 25 miles (40 km) to the northeast, scientists said.

Montserrat, a teardrop-shaped, 11-by-7-mile (18-by-11-km) island in the eastern Caribbean, lived in harmony with its dormant volcano for nearly four centuries before the mountain burst to life in July 1995.
Since then, Montserratians have been evacuated from the south end to the northern safe zone three times and more than half the population has left the island.
The British government said on Tuesday it hoped to reverse the exodus by developing the northern half.

"It is my own view that people who have left might well return when they know what our commitment is to the north," International Development Secretary Clare Short told a news conference in London after meeting Bertrand Osborne, Montserrat's chief minister.

Osborne said scientists believed that about 15-16 square miles (39-41 sq km) in the north would be safe, affording an opportunity for a planned development of the island with suitable housing and with a view to attracting industry.
Britain has given $60 million (37 million pounds) in assistance to Montserrat over the past year for food, road construction, housing and a hospital.
The island's airport, on the east coast, is closed and the only access is by ferry and helicopter from Antigua.
